1:
Aaron is named alongside Moses though he was left out of the preceding law, and both Gill and Ellicott give the same reason: these regulations chiefly concerned the priests, whose business it was to examine the symptoms and decide. Henry presses the oddity that follows — the thing was reckoned an uncleanness rather than a disease, which is why the law employed priests and not physicians, and why Christ is said to cleanse lepers rather than cure them. Wesley puts the office plainly: the priest was to admit to or exclude from the sanctuary. Calvin takes the same fact for evidence of intent. That God appointed judges from the priesthood, and only from its highest order, shows that his spiritual service was in view rather than mere bodily health; he grants that leprosy is contagious and that separating the infected was expedient, but denies this was the main object, since physicians would in time have judged better by art, whereas God gave the decision to the priests alone.

The signs are set out three times over. Clarke traces the Greek name to a word for a scale, since the body was often covered with thin white scales, whence Moses' hand and Miriam and Gehazi are called leprous as snow; the Hebrew name he derives from a verb to smite, whose cognate roots mean to cast down and to cause to cease, because the disease prostrates a man and obliges him to cease from all work. Keil and Delitzsch render the three Hebrew terms as a lifting up, an eruption from a root meaning to pour out, and a bright swollen spot from a root meaning to shine. Ellicott adds the colours the later authorities assigned: the swelling like an egg-shell, the glossy pimple white as snow.

Two marks decide the case. Keil and Delitzsch note that the hair which distinguished the Israelites was dark, so its turning white on the spot was the first sign, and the second was the spot appearing sunken below the surrounding skin; among the Arabs, they add, the disease is still reckoned curable while the hair on the white patches stays black. Ellicott records the stricter later rule that at least two hairs must be white. Wesley reads the change of colour as evidence of corrupt humours and of the weakness of nature.

The grammarians stop at the idiom of the verdict, which is literally make him unclean. Ellicott explains it by the usage in which a man is said to do what he officially declares done, as Ezekiel destroys the city whose destruction he only foretold; Calvin says the form establishes the dignity of the judgment, as though it proceeded from God himself; and Clarke makes it the proper measure of binding and loosing, an office of declaring the truth rather than any power to cleanse or pollute.

The delay is the last thing, and everyone moralises it. The suspected man is shut up seven days and, if nothing has altered, seven more. Wesley says the interval was for greater assurance, and Henry draws the same lesson, that neither ministers nor people should be rash in censure nor judge anything before the time. Calvin makes moderation the point — no one still curable should be condemned before his time — and then turns the passage against the canonists, who inferred a bishop's jurisdiction from the chief priest's, so that the bishop's official calls in physicians and pronounces what he confesses he does not know himself; and who, since the sin under which all labour is a spiritual leprosy, make absolution the cure and confession necessary. Reason runs the other way, for God gave the priest cognizance only of symptoms already manifest; the true analogy is excommunication. Even so, Henry and Wesley note that the man pronounced clean still washed his clothes: the acquitted prisoner goes down on his knees.
9:
What kind of case this second one is gets two answers. Ellicott takes it for leprosy re-appearing after cure, which is why a different treatment is enjoined. Keil and Delitzsch and Gill read the same phrase as an old, long-standing complaint rather than a return: Gill calls it inveterate and obstinate, not to be cured by medicine, which is why the man was sent to a priest and not a physician, and turns it at once to use — the leprosy of sin is an old disease, brought into the world with man and continuing from his youth upward, and nothing but grace and the blood of Christ removes it. Either way the procedure is the same, and Keil and Delitzsch mark what is distinctive: the evil being already established, the priest pronounced the man unclean immediately and did not shut him up at all.

Two signs establish it. Keil and Delitzsch and Wesley both read a white rising that has turned the hair white, together with raw flesh standing in the elevation; Wesley notes that the raw flesh showed the complaint had eaten into the flesh itself, which is why the next verse calls it old. Ellicott takes the two as alternatives, either of which suffices, and restricts the first: white hair indicates the disorder only while it coexists with the swelling that discoloured it. On the second he is fuller. The phrase the English gives as quick raw flesh means literally the quickening of live flesh, and the later authorities understood it as sound flesh — a patch resuming the appearance of life after the general whiteness had paled it — requiring a spot at least the size of a lentil. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the same Hebrew noun as properly meaning sustenance, and so that which shows life.

Then comes the paradox of the chapter, and the commentators divide over it. If the eruption covers the whole skin from head to foot, as far as the priest's eye can reach, the man is clean. Gill renders the Hebrew as if flowering it flowers, the man looking like a plant covered with white blossom. Keil and Delitzsch call this complete and rapid eruption the crisis of the disease, the diseased matter having turned itself into a scurf. Wesley explains it humorally: while the plague appeared in one part only it betrayed an ill humour lurking within and nature's inability to expel it, but once it overspread the whole it showed nature conquering the distemper and driving the humours out to the surface. Clarke asks the question directly — why is the partial leper unclean and the wholly covered man clean? — and answers from contagion. There are two stages, one covering the body with a dry white scurf and the other showing raw flesh in the risings; contact with raw flesh could carry the infection, since the ichor would be taken up by another's absorbent vessels, whereas a dry surface offered nothing to imbibe. He adds a speculation of his own: since the plague infected bodies, clothes and even house walls, was it not caused by animalcula burrowing under the skin?

The rule is then reversed once more. Should sound flesh reappear among the whiteness, the man is unclean again, the disease not having exhausted itself. Ellicott insists it is the sound flesh only, and not the white hair, that defiles here. Wesley says the point is repeated because living flesh looks like a sign of health, so that a priest might be deceived, and finds the principle in the mixture, a variety of colours being evidence of the plague while one colour continuing was a sign of soundness. Ellicott draws a last inference from the phrasing: because the text says in the day when sound flesh appears, the later administrators concluded there were days on which no examination was undertaken at all.
18:
The third case begins from an injury rather than from nothing. Ellicott takes it as leprosy developing out of a boil or inflammation that had apparently healed, and reports the later definition that fixed what sort of hurt was meant: a stroke from a piece of wood or a stone, or contact with pitch or hot water — deliberately distinguished from the burn by actual fire that follows. Gill preserves the same distinction from his own rabbinic sources, where the question what is an ulcer is answered by a blow from wood, stone, pitch or hot water. Clarke reaches for the medical nomenclature of his own day, reporting a conjecture that the phlegmonic, erysipelatous, gangrenous and phagedenic ulcers are all in view, every one brought before the priest to see whether it was infectious; and he adds that a man already carrying a sore was likelier to catch an infection than one whose skin was whole.

Henry, whose comment surveys this and the two cases that follow it, is interested in the moral shape of all three at once. When old sores that seemed to be cured break out again, he says, it is to be feared there is a leprosy in them — such is the danger of those who, having escaped the pollutions of the world, are entangled in them again and overcome. The burn that comes next he reads as an accident, and finds in it that the burning of strife and contention often occasions the rising of a corruption which witnesses to men's faces that they are unclean. Of the scall on the head he notes that the judgment turned on a very small matter, black hair being a sign of soundness and yellow an indication of the plague. Reading through the catalogue of ailments, he draws two duties: to lament the calamitous state of human life, beset on every side by troops of diseases which all entered by sin, and to give thanks where God has afflicted us with none of them, since a healthful constitution binds us to glorify God with our bodies.

The procedure itself turns on the same two marks as before, with one addition. Ellicott notes that a white-reddish colour is peculiar to a re-opened scar and therefore has not been mentioned until now, and passes on the later description of it as having the appearance of red wine poured into water, either a palish white or somewhat darker. If the priest finds the spot lower than the surrounding skin and the hair upon it turned white — the two critical symptoms — he declares it leprosy at once. Where both are absent, Ellicott points out that the quarantine is only a single week here rather than two. Keil and Delitzsch describe what the priest then looks for: if the spot has spread during those seven days it is leprosy, but if it has stood in its place and not spread, it is what the Hebrew calls the closing or the burning of the abscess, meaning that part of the skin killed by the inflammation, which gradually falls away as scurf. Wesley notes only that the word rendered dark may as well be rendered contracted.

The verdict rests on spreading, and both grammarians say why. Ellicott holds that a spot which spreads proves the blood vitiated and the distemper already developing in the body, whereas a spot that stays exactly as it was shows the thing to be no more than the re-opening of the old boil, and the man is pronounced clear of leprosy. He notices in passing that the word leprosy has dropped out of the Hebrew at one point where the ancient versions still preserve it. Gill records a dissenting rabbinic reading of the spreading, referred not to the skin of the flesh but to the ulcer itself.
24:
The fourth case is a burn, and the first business of the commentators is to say how it differs from the third. Ellicott is precise about it. The previous case covered a hurt from pitch or hot water; this one specifies a sore, pustule or blister raised by what the margin rightly calls a burning of fire rather than, as the text has it, a hot burning. He quotes the ancient canons as defining it distinctly — that which is burnt with a coal or with embers, whatsoever comes from the force of actual fire — in express contradistinction to the inflammation already dealt with. Gill gives the same definition from the same tradition, answering the question what is a burning with whatever is burnt by a coal or by hot ashes, and so whatever sore or blister is occasioned by fire touching the part or by anything heated in fire. Wesley puts it most simply, a burning by the touch of hot iron or of burning coals, which naturally makes the ulcer in which the suspect spot then appears.

What grows on the scar is described with the same care. Ellicott renders the phrase the English gives as the quick flesh that burneth as the sound flesh of the burning, meaning the tender new flesh that forms once the purulent matter has drained away, and it is on this that the symptoms show themselves. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same thing as the life of the scar — the skin forming upon the scar of the burn — becoming a whitish red or a white spot, that is, rising into a bright swollen patch; and where a verdict later speaks of a rising of the burn, they gloss it as a rising of the flesh and skin growing out of the scar.

Beyond that, the striking fact is that the law simply repeats itself, and the commentators say so rather than inventing distinctions. Keil and Delitzsch state flatly that this case was to be treated exactly like the one before it. Ellicott, coming to the clause where the two decisive marks are named, does no more than point back: the hair that was black has now turned white, and the appearance of the spot is deeper than the surrounding skin, both already explained. When those marks are absent he refers the reader to the directions given for the boil, the same seven days of seclusion and the same second inspection. Wesley likewise glosses the closing verdict by pointing back to the burning mentioned at the head of the case, and nothing more.

Two small procedural notes survive from the repetition. Ellicott observes that where the two symptoms are present the priest declares leprosy at once, the burn having merely furnished the occasion for a disease already in the body; where they are absent the doubt is resolved by waiting. Gill supplies the more practical point about the waiting itself. When the seventh day is come the priest may look at any time during that day; he need not wait until its end, nor until the seven days are precisely up — and Gill adds that the same is to be understood everywhere in this chapter where the like expression is used, which is as near as any of these voices comes to acknowledging how often the chapter says the same thing over again.
29:
The plague on the head or the chin is a separate case because its sign is a different colour. Ellicott notes that the distemper attacking the hairy parts first is not uncommon, and Gill takes the wording generously, covering a man's beard or a woman's head alike. Clarke reports the Jewish understanding that the disease made the hair drop out by the roots, and Ellicott confirms it from the canons, which define the term the English renders dry scall as an affection leaving the place quite bare. Calvin keeps this apart from ordinary baldness. What is spoken of is not the baldness of old age, nor hair lost through some indisposition, neither of which pollutes a man, but the loss that follows on leprosy; and because some kinds do not differ greatly from it at first sight — the creeping kind that leaves the scalp smooth in winding tracks like a serpent's folds, and the scurf named from the fox — the distinction had to be drawn. He adds that the Arabian poets called a forehead baldness noble, as coming of the helmet, and the hinder sort servile.

The decisive sign is yellow hair, and Ellicott and Wesley both mark the reversal. Elsewhere the hair whitens; here the naturally black hair turns golden and grows short. Ellicott gives the later description of the colour — like the new plumage of young pigeons, or thin gold — and the rule that followed: the sign is the hair becoming short, so that long hair, though as yellow as gold, is no mark of uncleanness. Keil and Delitzsch add the other symptom, the spot appearing deeper than the skin.

Where black hair remains, the doubt is over. Wesley says that had black appeared it would have ended the question, black being a sign of soundness and strength of nature as yellow was of unsoundness. Ellicott defends the Hebrew against an emendation: the text says there is no black hair in it, which he treats as another way of saying there is yellow hair, and he argues that yellow on a first inspection was suspicious without being conclusive, since hair sometimes turns yellow temporarily in an ordinary ulcer and returns to black as the patient recovers, so that the absence of black warranted quarantine rather than a verdict. Those who follow the Greek in reading yellow for black have changed it worse than unnecessarily: on that reading both unfavourable symptoms would be missing, and the priest would have had to pronounce the man clean outright.

Then the shaving. The head and beard are shaved so that any change can be seen, Wesley says for the more certain discovery of the plague's growth or stay, and Ellicott notes it was done by professional barbers. But the scall itself is left unshaved, so that the colour of the hair on it stays visible; Ellicott describes shaving everything round it except two hairs on each side, by which the priest could tell whether it was spreading. Clarke gives a different reason — that shaving would inflame the place, so that it might take on appearances other than leprosy and leave the priest unable to judge.

The verdicts close the case, and one is provisional. Gill dates the second inspection to the thirteenth day from the first, and Ellicott says that if no symptom has appeared by then the man is pronounced clean. Yet Gill observes that the plague might still spread afterwards, so that the priest looks a fourth time; and in that event, Keil and Delitzsch and Wesley agree, he need not search for yellow hair at all, the spreading being proof enough. If instead the spot has stood still and black hair has grown up in it, the scall is healed — Ellicott recording the last refinement, two black hairs at least, long enough for the tip to bow towards the root.
38:
The fifth case exists in order to acquit somebody. Ellicott calls it the harmless leprosy, which does not render the patient unclean at all, and describes the spots as of unequal size and standing a little above the skin, appearing generally on the neck and face, and — the decisive point — leaving the colour of the hair unchanged. Gill notes that the law respects man and woman alike. Keil and Delitzsch are the fullest, because they can still name the thing: the eruption comes out in white rings, and if these are dull or pale it is the harmless complaint the Arabs still call bahak, a word the Hebrew itself preserves; they describe pale rings which do not touch the hair, cause no inconvenience, and last from two months to two years. Ellicott adds that the disorder still prevails in the East under that same biblical name, being a white eruption which runs a few months and disappears of itself. Wesley's only contribution is on the word for the colour, which he would render contracted, or confined to the place where the spots are.

Henry treats this provision and the one that follows it as a pair of safeguards, and draws the general rule from them: neither a freckled skin nor a bald head was to be mistaken for a leprosy, for every deformity must not forthwith be made a ceremonial defilement. He remembers that Elisha was jeered for his bald head, and observes that it was the children of Bethel, who knew not the judgments of their God, who turned that baldness into a reproach — the law itself had expressly declined to.

Against that background Henry marks how sharply the law turns when the plague does appear in a bald head, where the verdict is that the man is utterly unclean and his plague is in his head. He reads the emphasis spiritually and without softening it. If the leprosy of sin has seized the head, so that the judgment is corrupted and wicked principles are embraced which countenance and support wicked practices, that is an utter uncleanness, and few are ever cleansed of it; whereas soundness in the faith keeps the leprosy out of the head and saves the conscience from being shipwrecked.

Henry's comment then runs ahead to what becomes of a man once convicted. The leprosy was not itself a sin, he insists, but a sad token of God's displeasure: a reproach to the man's name, a full stop to his business, a severance from his friends, an exclusion from the sanctuary, and in effect the ruin of every comfort he could have had in this world — a condition Henry thinks the psalmist Heman either shared or alludes to. From this he takes the convicted man's cry as the pattern of penitence: he must not insist upon his cleanness once the priest has spoken, but justify God and accept the punishment of his iniquity, the rent clothes and covered lip being tokens of that shame which should fill the hearts of penitents.

The second use of the cry Henry keeps carefully distinct from the first. The leper had also to warn others off, calling to anyone he saw at a distance to take heed of touching him — not, Henry is careful to say, because the leprosy was catching, but because ceremonial uncleanness was contracted by the touch of a leper, so that the leper himself had to give notice of the danger. And this was all the law could do, being weak through the flesh: it taught the leper to cry Unclean, unclean. The gospel has put another cry into the lepers' mouths, for the ten who met Christ lifted up their voices to ask for mercy instead. The law only shows us our disease; the gospel shows us our help.
40:
The last case concerns a bald head, and it opens by conceding that baldness is no disease at all. Ellicott notes that although baldness was reckoned a disgrace and often taken for a divine punishment, the mere falling of the hair is no sign of the plague. Two kinds are then distinguished. Gill and Ellicott both follow the rabbinic definition of the first as loss from the crown backwards to the neck and of the second as loss forwards to the forehead and temples, and Ellicott would render them baldness of the backhead and of the forehead. Keil and Delitzsch give the same words the same senses and state the conclusion plainly: bald heads of both kinds were naturally clean.

What defiles is what grows on the bald place. Keil and Delitzsch describe a white reddish mole forming on the bare scalp, recognised by its having the appearance of leprosy on the skin of the body, in which case the man was unclean. Ellicott makes the resemblance more exact by pointing back to the boil: the eruption here is like the one arising in a healed sore. Wesley states the inference the law is drawing — such an eruption shows that this baldness came not from age nor accident, but from the leprosy.

Ellicott then notices what the law does not say. The reddish-white rising is the only symptom named, and nothing is said about remanding a doubtful case as in every other instance; but because the text says the rising is in appearance like the leprosy in the skin of the flesh, the authorities inferred that all the criteria given for the one are implied in the other, and supplied the missing procedure — sound flesh makes the man unclean at once, and where there is none he is shut up and examined at the week's end, and if the spot has spread he is unclean, and if not he is shut up a second week. Ellicott adds the reason why only two marks operate here: on a bald scalp white hair cannot be among the criteria at all. Gill notices a restriction of another kind, that the law speaks only of a leprous man because women did not commonly grow bald.

Calvin takes up the verdict and reads its two halves as doing different work. The first declares the man unclean; the second charges the priest to pass sentence, so that the uncleanness should not be carried into the congregation. The words his plague is upon his head mean, he says, that the man is sentenced to a just ignominy, Moses taking it for granted that God holds up to public infamy whomever he smites with leprosy. The verses that follow give the form in which that sentence is executed: the rent garment as the mark of disgrace, the bare head, the covered mouth, the man made the proclaimer of his own pollution, and the dwelling outside the camp — which last, Calvin observes, describes the people's condition in the desert, since once settled in the land they drove lepers out of the towns instead.

On two details he declines the obvious explanation. Of the covered lip he does not know whether the opinion of those who make it a guard against infecting others by the breath is sound; his own view is that because such men were civilly dead they bore the symbol of death in a covered face. And on the cry he takes a position against a possible reading: some construe the verb passively, so that the man shall be called unclean, and Calvin allows the form often carries that force, but because the repetition is emphatic he thinks the lepers warned everyone with their own mouths not to approach them. He hears Jeremiah alluding to this very passage when the cry over a polluted city is, Depart ye, depart ye.
45:
Every voice here reads the leper's dress as mourning. Clarke has him appear as one that mourned for the dead: clothes rent in token of extreme sorrow, the head made bare by leaving off the turban, and a covering on the upper lip made by tying up the jaws with a linen cloth in the very manner the Jews bind up their dead — a custom still kept at funerals among the Jews of Barbary. Ellicott agrees, and gives the reason: leprosy was regarded as a visitation from God for the sufferer's own sin. He would render the second sign not head bare but hair dishevelled, and reads the covering of the lip as the veiling of the beard. Keil and Delitzsch summarise the prescription in the same terms.

Wesley divides the purpose of each sign in two, and the division is his own contribution. The clothes were rent in the upper and fore parts, which are the most visible, partly as a token of sorrow — for though the disease was not a sin it was an effect of sin, cutting the man off from converse with men and from the enjoyment of God in his ordinances — and partly as a warning to others. The bare head was another sign of mourning, God requiring men to be deeply sensible of his judgments though not overwhelmed by them. The covering on the lip was partly a further badge of shame and partly, he thinks, for the preservation of others from the man's breath. And the cry served three ends: it begged the pity of others, confessed his own infirmity, and cautioned those who came near.

On the cry the commentators differ about who made it. Clarke takes it as the leper's own warning, given to prevent anyone coming near lest the contagion be diffused through society, and notes that the Targum renders the words as a caution to others rather than a confession — be not ye made unclean. Ellicott explains why so strong a warning was needed: the very entrance of a leper into a house rendered everything in it unclean. He records that in some instances the work was done not by the man himself but by a herald going before him.

Henry keeps the emphasis on what the sentence cost. Once the priest had pronounced him unclean it put a stop to his business, cut him off from friends and relations, and ruined all his comfort; and the man's part was to humble himself, not insisting on his cleanness now that the priest had spoken, but accepting the punishment. The exclusion Henry reads as a type: shut out of the camp, and later out of the city where he lived, to dwell with none but lepers like himself, the leper prefigures the purity that ought to be kept in the gospel church.

Ellicott documents how far the seclusion was carried, first in the later Jewish law and then in Christendom. Under the second Temple a leper standing beneath a tree defiled a clean man who passed; a synagogue had to make him a separate compartment; and the disease was reckoned a living death. These rabbinic laws, Ellicott says, were imported into the medieval Church, where a priest in his stole led the afflicted man into church, had him exchange his clothes for a black garment, and read the service for the dead over him; he was then taken to a sequestered house, earth was thrown on his feet as a sign of burial, and he forfeited inheritance as a dead man. Wesley gives three reasons for the solitude: humiliation, the prevention of infection, and a lesson on the danger of company with spiritual lepers. Keil and Delitzsch note that the separation lasted as long as the disease did, and Gill that throughout those days the man was reckoned unclean and avoided as such.
47:
Leprosy in a garment divides these commentators more sharply than anything else in the chapter, because they cannot agree what it was. Gill sets out the question: whether it proceeded from natural causes or was miraculous and peculiar to the Jews. The Hebrew writers generally asserted the second, but Gill reports that Abarbinel thought it might come by contact with a leprous person, and he is drawn to that himself, since the matter adhering to cloth will work between the threads and corrode the texture. Clarke takes a third line: the garment was fretted, and was therefore likely attacked by small animals of the kind that produce the itch, breeding in the cloth and corroding it like moths. Keil and Delitzsch propose a fourth, that it was nothing but mildew, arising from damp and want of air, showing in linen as round coloured spots which eat the fabric until it falls to pieces, and in leather as holes eaten in.

Ellicott refutes two of these by name. Since the same phrase is used of garments and of human beings, and the symptoms and course are identical, he holds it beyond doubt that the same distemper is meant; so the reading which makes it vermin fretting the cloth runs against the uniform sense of the phrase and against the testimony of the men who handled the disease, who assure us it was a sign and a miracle in Israel. Equally untenable, he says, is the theory that it was an infectious condition caught from leprous matter — and here he makes a larger claim, that neither these regulations nor the later canons treat leprosy as contagious at all. His evidence is cumulative: the priest was in close contact with the leper; the man wholly covered was pronounced clean and free to mix with the community; everything was carried out of an infected house before the priest entered, so that it might be used again; and by the canons a leprous child or foreigner defiled nobody.

Henry and Wesley decline the dispute. Henry says the thing is altogether unaccountable to us now and that the learned confess it was a sign and a miracle in Israel, an extraordinary punishment marking displeasure against a person or family. Wesley adds that Moses would hardly have courted his people's contempt by legislating about a fiction their own experience refuted.

On the warp and the woof the difficulty is mechanical. Gill reports Castalio's rendering of the outer and the inner side of the cloth, but prefers to take the terms as the yarn itself, before it is wrought together in the loom and, as the Jews say, while still upon the spindle; Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion by answering the objection that warp and weft could not be infected separately once woven. Wesley holds that if the words are doubtful now it is not material to us, the law being abolished. On the colours, Gill notes a disagreement over whether the doubled Hebrew forms weaken the sense or strengthen it, one authority making them merely greenish and reddish and another exceeding green and red.

The procedure then runs by the familiar steps, and Ellicott marks each parallel with the human case: a week's quarantine, spreading as the decisive sign, and the leprous garment defiling by contact just as a human leper did. Where it has spread the thing is burnt, since the disorder can never be got out of stuffs. Clarke supports that from experience, reporting that garments infected by the itch have communicated the disease six or seven years later, as the sorters of rags at paper mills have found. Gill records that the burning was done outside the city. Henry notes the safeguard at the other end: the garment was not burnt on suspicion but had to be shown to the priest, since sentence must never be given upon a surmise.
53:
Where the spot has not spread, the cloth gets a second chance, and the steps are set out with the same patience as for a man. Gill notes that the priest ordered the washing rather than performing it, and Clarke explains the further seven days as time for the contagion to declare itself unequivocally. Keil and Delitzsch describe what follows if the mole has turned pale by the end of that second week: the place of it was torn out, and the fabric was then washed a second time, after which it was clean. Clarke reports the rabbinic account of the two washings — the first to put away the plague, the second to cleanse.

Ellicott takes the harder verdict first. If the spot keeps its suspicious colour after washing, the thing must be burnt even though it has not spread, the retained colour being itself the sign. He then glosses the obscure phrase that justifies this: properly, it is a corroding in the fore baldness thereof or in the back baldness thereof — the law borrowing the vocabulary of the bald head to distinguish the upper face of the fabric from the under. Though the plague has not widened, it has eaten inward. Where instead the colour has darkened and the spot contracted, Ellicott has the affected piece cut out and burnt and the garment pronounced clean; and if the plague then breaks out in another part, the whole must be destroyed, the disorder being incurable in stuffs. Keil and Delitzsch agree that a reappearance after the tearing out was leprosy bursting forth afresh.

Ellicott is careful about what the double washing means for a garment that survives. The suspicious symptoms often disappeared once the stuff had been washed and quarantined, showing it had not been real leprosy; but even so it had to be washed again before it could be pronounced fit for use. Gill sees in that washing a figure of the garments of men washed in the blood of Christ, and on the closing formula both he and Ellicott say the same thing plainly: these are the rules by which priests were to judge cloth clean or unclean.

Calvin, coming to the end of the chapter, declines to go through it. This kind of disease, he says, God in his clemency has willed to be unknown to us. He has subjected woollen garments to the moth and vessels to rust, surrounding the human race with rottenness so that everywhere our eyes should light upon the punishment of sin; but what the leprosy of garments may be is simply unknown. Its expiation taught his ancient people to beware even of external uncleanness, so as to cleanse themselves from all filthiness of flesh and spirit. It has seemed to him sufficient to touch upon the sum of the matter — it is not his purpose to perform the office of the grammarian.

Clarke closes in the opposite manner, with the longest sustained comparison in the chapter. Both Jews and Gentiles, he says, have taken the leprosy for an emblem of sin, and he runs the parallel in seven steps: the disease began from a hidden infection, was conspicuous, spread over the body, reached clothes and habitation, rendered a man loathsome, obliged his separation, and required him to proclaim his own uncleanness. Against each he sets its counterpart — the corruption of nature as the hidden spring of all transgression, and the sinner infectious as well as infected, spreading the contagion by precept and example. It is only the universality of the evil, Clarke observes, that keeps sinners from being expelled as monsters: ten lepers could keep company because they shared one infection, and civil society holds because it is itself a leprous community. The remedy is the last step — whoever would be saved must humble himself, confess, and bring the sacrifice by which guilt is taken away.
